findings.title: HMAC_DRBG Generate does not enforce the SP 800-90A request or reseed interval limits
findings.standardsReference: NIST SP 800-90A Rev. 1, Table 2 and Generate requirements
findings.evidence: Generate accepts any positive Int32 byte count, never rejects reseed_counter above 2^48, and the CSPRNG-1.2 sample generator requested 1,048,576 bytes per call rather than the 65,536-byte maximum.
findings.consequence: The reusable production runtime and qualification invocation are not fully SP 800-90A-conforming. Canonical game sampling currently requests only eight bytes per call, so no observed production outcome is shown biased or predictable, but the standards claim and qualification baseline are materially affected.
findings.remediation: Create a new qualified source version that rejects Generate requests above 65,536 bytes and requires reseed after 2^48 requests. Change the qualification generator to conforming chunks and define the statistical requalification scope without deleting prior evidence.

findings.title: Instantiation and reseed parameter enforcement permits unsupported security claims and undersized inputs
findings.standardsReference: NIST SP 800-90A Rev. 1, Sections 8.6.7, 10.1 and Table 2
findings.evidence: Instantiate accepts every security strength at least 128, including SHA-256 requests above 256 or non-table values; it does not enforce a nonce requirement. Reseed does not verify entropy length against the session security strength.
findings.consequence: The canonical production caller supplies defensible fixed parameters, but the registered reusable runtime can report success for nonconforming instantiation or reseed inputs. That is a material misuse and conformance defect in the qualified implementation boundary.
findings.remediation: In a new qualified baseline, enforce permitted strengths, hash-specific maximums, nonce requirements, and minimum reseed entropy before changing state.

findings.title: Existing 'official' HMAC_DRBG vectors are not traceable to authoritative CAVP vector identities
findings.standardsReference: NIST CAVP DRBG validation evidence practice
findings.evidence: The fixtures cover SHA-256/384/512, instantiate, Generate, reseed, additional input, consecutive Generate operations, and final Key/V, but use Mosera-created sequential inputs and no CAVP vector set or COUNT provenance.
findings.consequence: They are useful deterministic regression fixtures, not proof of CAVP validation or independently sourced algorithm conformance.
findings.remediation: Add traceable NIST/CAVP vectors with source artifact hashes and identifiers as qualification-only tests; preserve the existing fixtures under an accurate name.

findings.title: Production evidence persists an unnecessary hash of secret initialization material
findings.standardsReference: Secret minimization and evidence-boundary review requirement
findings.evidence: SeedIdentifier is SHA-256(entropy || nonce || personalization) and is persisted. The older, currently unwired production evidence contract also defines persisted nonce_hash and seed_commitment_hash fields.
findings.consequence: No practical preimage attack is identified against 80 bytes of OS-sourced material, but the verifier provides no entropy-quality proof and unnecessarily fingerprints secret initialization inputs.
findings.remediation: Version the evidence schema to remove secret-derived identifiers. Retain non-secret draw/execution IDs, source/provider/configuration versions, timestamps, health results, output/result hashes, and certificate links.

findings.title: Exceptional entropy-provider paths do not always zero temporary managed buffers
findings.standardsReference: NIST SP 800-90A state/secret protection and defense in depth
findings.evidence: Linux chunk zeroization and all readiness probe zeroization occur after successful Fill rather than in finally blocks.
findings.consequence: A failed call may leave temporary bytes in managed memory until garbage collection. No persistence or log leakage was found.
findings.remediation: Zero temporary chunks and readiness probes in finally blocks in the next qualified source version.

findings.title: Bounded integer byte order is platform-dependent
findings.consequence: Uniformity is unaffected, and deployed/qualified targets are little-endian. Fixed-input deterministic results would differ on a future big-endian target.
findings.remediation: Use an explicit endian conversion in a future qualified baseline and pin supported production architectures.

findings.title: Cancellation can prevent append of non-authoritative failure-attempt evidence
findings.evidence: OperationCanceledException is excluded from failure recording, and a canceled token is reused for append after other failures.
findings.consequence: Locks and secrets are still released and no result is authoritative before atomic completion, but canceled/failed pre-commit attempts may have incomplete audit evidence.
findings.remediation: Use a bounded cleanup token for non-secret failure evidence and define cancellation attempt semantics without persisting partial random output.

findings.title: SP 800-90B entropy assurance is an external platform dependency
findings.evidence: Mosera verifies API support and successful reads but has no platform entropy characterization, min-entropy estimate, or validation certificate.
findings.consequence: Claims must be limited to requesting OS cryptographic entropy; SP 800-90B compliance and 256 bits of validated entropy assurance are unsupported.
findings.remediation: For external certification, select a validated platform/module boundary or obtain accepted vendor/laboratory evidence.

findings.title: SP 800-90C RBG2 is the closest architecture, but formal classification lacks evidence
findings.evidence: Mosera combines an OS source with HMAC_DRBG instantiate/reseed, but has not established a validated entropy source and DRBG in the required RBG security boundary.
findings.remediation: Resolve the 90A blockers and validated entropy/module boundary before making a 90C claim.

findings.title: Managed-runtime zeroization cannot guarantee physical erasure of all copies
findings.evidence: Explicit arrays are zeroed, but HMAC constructors/runtime internals, garbage collector movement, crash dumps, and debugger snapshots can retain copies outside application control.
findings.consequence: The implementation demonstrates best-effort logical zeroization, not guaranteed physical memory erasure.
findings.remediation: Carry this limitation into external review and harden host dump/debug access.
